column2: Seen and asked again, "What did the thigh-born one say to you?", the Siddha replied, "I do not know; Urvashi herself told me she does not know you."
Hearing the Siddha's words, the brahmin, his lips parted in a smile, said again, "Ask Urvashi this: 'How might you come to know him?'"
Very well, I will do so, said the Siddha, and went to heaven; there he saw Urvashi coming out of Shakra's palace.
The excellent Siddha spoke to her, and she said to the Siddha, "Let that best of brahmins undertake some vow;
by that act I shall come to know him, O Siddha, and not otherwise." The Siddha returned with Urvashi's words to that foolish brahmin
and told him, and the brahmin declared this vow: "Before you, O perfected one, I make this vow:
from today I will not eat a shakata-cake; this I declare truly." Told this, the Siddha went to heaven, saw Urvashi,
and said, "From today he will never eat a shakata-cake." Urvashi said to the Siddha, "Now I know him —
by the very vow he took, the fool who mocks me." Having said this, Narayana's daughter quickly went to her dwelling.
The Siddha too roamed the earth at will. And Urvashi, the lovely one, went to the city of Varanasi
and bathed in the water of the Matsyodari, wearing a divine form. Then the fool too went to the river Matsyodari, O sage,
and saw Urvashi bathing there. On seeing her, a powerful, unsettling desire grew strong in him.
The fool made advances, and Urvashi herself recognized him; knowing him to be the fool the Siddha had spoken of, she smiled and said to him:
What do you want from me, fortunate one? Say it quickly here. I will do as you say; you may speak freely.
Save my life by giving yourself to me, sweetly smiling one.
Then Urvashi said to the brahmin, "I am keeping a vow just now; wait here a moment, and await my return."
I will wait, said the brahmin, and she went to heaven. After a month she returned and saw the brahmin grown thin,
having stayed a month on the river bank without food. Seeing his resolve, the celestial woman then took the form of an old woman
and made on the river bank a shakata-cake covered with sugar, with ghee and honey, and went to the river Matsyodari.
After bathing, staying on the ground with the cake, the lovely-eyed one called that brahmin and said:
I have kept a severe vow, O brahmin, for the sake of good fortune; at the end of the vow I must give the concluding gift. Accept it, O brahmin.
He said, "What is this sugar-covered thing that is being given? My throat is parched with hunger, so I ask; tell me truly, good lady."
She said, "It is a shakata-cake, O brahmin, made with sugar and flour. Take it and refresh your life at once."
Hearing that, he remembered, and though tormented by hunger he said, "Good lady, I will not take it, for I have made a vow
before the company of Siddhas not to eat a shakata-cake, so that Urvashi might know me. Give it to someone else."
She said, "Good man, you made the vow about a wooden cart (shakata); this is not made of wood. Eat it, for you are sorely tormented by hunger."
The brahmin replied to her, "I made no such distinction, good lady; my vow was made in general terms."
The slender one said to him again, "If you will not eat it, brahmin, take it and go home; your family will eat it."
He said to her, "Fair-toothed one, I will not go home yet. A lovely woman came here, surpassing all in the three worlds in her qualities;
tormented by love, I entreated her, and she reassured me: 'Wait here a moment.' And I said, 'I will wait.'
She has been gone a month, good lady, and I have stayed, devoted to truth, keeping my vow for the sake of union with her."
Hearing his words, Urvashi took on her own supreme form, laughed with deep feeling, and said to the brahmin:

Well done, brahmin! With a steadfast mind you have kept your vow truly, holding fast in your wish to see me.
brahmapuran:228:144	I am Urvashi herself, brahmin; I came to test you. You have been tested and proved resolute — you are a sage whose austerity is truth, Satyatapas.
brahmapuran:228:145	Go to the region of Shukarava, to the tirtha famed as Rupatirtha; you will attain perfection, best of brahmins, and then you will win me.
Having said this, Urvashi flew up to heaven, O brahmins, and that brahmin Satyatapas went to Rupatirtha.
There, devoted to peace, keeping vows and disciplines and pure, when he gave up his body he went to the excellent world of the Gandharvas.
Having enjoyed pleasures there for a hundred manvantaras, he was born a king in a good family, devoted to pleasing his subjects.
He performed various sacrifices completed with excellent fees; then, entrusting the kingdom to his sons, he went again to Shaukarava.
Dying once more at Rupatirtha, he went to Shakra's world; having enjoyed pleasures there for a hundred manvantaras, he fell from it
and in the excellent city of Pratishthana was born as Pururavas, son of Budha, for union with Urvashi, O ascetics.
Thus of old the brahmin Satyatapas, at the famous tirtha named Rupa, worshipped Vishnu in birth after birth, obtained enjoyments, and then attained liberation.
Then he said to his father, "Father, I have resolved to live up to my name; I have openly taken up the Vaishnava way that protects."
His father, coming to him, said, "This is not dharma, my son; a wise man should not refuse to take a wife.
Do as I say, son, for I am your father and your master; do not let my family sink into hell through the end of our line."
Hearing his father's command, the self-controlled son, remembering with joy the ancient wonder of worldly existence, said to him:

Listen, father, to my words, true and well reasoned: one should live up to one's name — that is true, O king.
brahmapuran:229:32	I have passed through thousands of births and hundreds of old ages and deaths, and every kind of union with wives and separation from them.
brahmapuran:229:33	Grass, shrub, creeper, vine, reptile, beast, bird, animal, woman, man and more — I have been these hundreds of times;
brahmapuran:229:34	Ganas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyadharas, great serpents, Yakshas, Guhyakas, Rakshasas, Danavas, Apsaras and gods;
brahmapuran:229:35	I have been a lord of rivers a thousand times, father, again and again; I have been created many times in creation and dissolved in dissolution.
brahmapuran:229:36	Such has been my mockery, father, while joined to a wife. Hear what happened in my third birth before this; I will tell you briefly, as it arises from the greatness of a tirtha.
brahmapuran:229:37	After passing through many births among men, gods, Gandharvas, great serpents, Vidyadharas, birds and Kinnaras, I was born in a family as the great sage Sutapas.
brahmapuran:229:38	Then there arose in me a great unshakable devotion to Janardana, lord of the world, slayer of Madhu; through various vows and fasts and devotion, the bearer of discus and mace was pleased.
brahmapuran:229:39	Pleased, the great-souled Vishnu, giver of boons, came to me mounted on the lord of birds and said in a loud voice, 'Choose a boon, brahmin; whatever you desire, I will give.'
brahmapuran:229:40	Then I said to Hari, the ruler: 'If you are pleased, Keshava, this is what I choose: that supreme maya of yours — I wish to know it, Janardana.'
brahmapuran:229:41	Then the enemy of Madhu and Kaitabha said to me, 'What do you want with that maya, brahmin? I will give you dharma, wealth and pleasure, excellent sons and freedom from illness.'
brahmapuran:229:42	Again I said to Murari, 'My only wish, beyond wealth and dharma, is to know this maya of yours; show it to me today, lotus-eyed one.'
brahmapuran:229:43	Then the Lord Vishnu, chief of man-lions, husband of Shri, said to me: 'No one knows my maya, nor will anyone ever know it.
brahmapuran:229:44	Formerly, brahmin, the divine sage named Narada, son of Brahma, was devoted to me; he too pleased me, just as you have, with his devotion.
brahmapuran:229:45	I gave him a boon and was going, and he too chose this very boon; though I dissuaded him, out of great folly he chose it, just as you have.
brahmapuran:229:46	Then I told him, Narada, plunge into the water and you will know my maya." Narada plunged into the water and became Sushila, daughter of the king of Kashi.
When she came of age she was given to Sudharma, son of the king of Vidarbha, a man of fine character; and the great sage, united with him, enjoyed incomparable pleasures.
When his father went to heaven, the valiant prince gladly took the kingdom that came to him by succession, and ruling Vidarbha he was surrounded by many sons and grandsons.
Then a great war broke out between King Sudharma and the lord of Kashi, and in it the king of Vidarbha and the king of Kashi perished in battle with their sons and grandsons.
Then Sushila, learning that her father had fallen with his sons and her husband with his sons and grandsons, left the city and went to the battlefield, and saw the great slaughter
in her husband's army and her father's army. Overcome with grief, she lamented long, and in her anguish went to her mother; then her brothers, sons, nephews and grandsons,
her husband and her father she took, and in the great cremation ground built a great pyre and herself set fire to it; when the fire had blazed up,
Sushila rushed into it, crying, "Ah my son, ah my son!" At that moment she became the sage Narada again, and the fire became as clear as crystal —
a full lake — and he came up out of it. Before him stood Keshava, best of gods, who, laughing, said to the divine sage Narada:
Who is your son? Tell me, great sage. Whom are you mourning as dead, your wits lost? Narada was filled with shame, and then I said to him again:
Such, Narada, is my painful maya; not even the lotus-seated Brahma and the others, with great Indra and Rudra, can know it; how will you know what is so hard to conceive?
Hearing this, the great sage said, "Give me devotion to you, Vishnu; and when my time comes, grant me remembrance of you, and let me always have sight of you, O Lord.
Where I, in my anguish, mounted the pyre today, let that be a tirtha, ever presided over by you, Keshava, destroyer of sin, together with the lotus-born Brahma."
Then I said to the brahmin Narada, "Let your pyre be a tirtha named Sitoda; I, Vishnu, will dwell here always, and Maheshvara will dwell to the north.
When the three-eyed one cuts off Brahma's head, which speaks harshly of me, then he will come to this tirtha of yours to be freed from the skull.
When the destroyer of Tripura bathes at this tirtha the skull will fall to the ground, and so it will become famous on earth as the tirtha Kapalamochana.
From then on the rider of the clouds will never leave that most holy, excellent tirtha; and there, brahmin, it is said, the fierce sin of brahmin-slaying has no hold in that sacred field.
Since the slayer of the gods' enemies will not leave that chief of sacred fields, rich in merit, the gods praised it as the secret tirtha Vimukta, merit-giving, called imperishable.
A man who has committed great sins, entering it pure and heedful, becomes purified when he meditates on me, and attains liberation by the Lord's grace.
Or, becoming there a Rudra-pishacha, he suffers sorrow in another birth; freed from sin after many years, he will be born in a brahmin's home.
Then, pure and self-controlled, at the hour of his death Rudra will recite to him the saving Taraka mantra." Having said this to Narada, best of brahmins, I went to the ocean of milk, my own home.
And that brahmin wandered in heaven, honoured by the king of the Gandharvas. This I have told you for your understanding: my maya cannot be known.
If you still wish to know it, then enter the water today and you shall know it.' Thus instructed by Hari, the brahmin, driven by what was to be, plunged into the water.
At Kokamukha, father, that brahmin then became a girl in an outcaste's house — beautiful, endowed with good conduct and virtues — and she grew up and reached youth.
She was married to Subahu, an outcaste's son devoid of beauty; her husband was not pleasing to her, though she was dear to him.
Two sons were born blind, and later a daughter who was deaf. Her husband was poor, and she, bewildered, would go to the river and weep there every day.
Once she took her pitcher and went, and entered the water to bathe; and at once the brahmin was himself again, of good conduct and devoted to the yoga of rites.
Her husband, thinking she had been gone long, went to the holy river to look; he saw the pitcher but not her on the bank, and in great grief he wept aloud.
Then the two blind sons and the deaf daughter came there in sorrow, and seeing their father weeping, they too wept bitterly in distress.
Then he asked the brahmins on the river bank, "Did you see a woman who came running for water? Tell me." They said, "She entered
the river and did not come out again; that is all we know." Hearing those dreadful words, he wept, his eyes flooded with tears of grief.
Seeing him weeping with his sons and daughter, I became deeply distressed; anguish seized me, and with it the memory, 'I was that outcaste woman,' O king.
Then I said to Matanga, O king, 'Why do you weep in such distress? Through great folly you will not get her back; what use is your wailing here?'
He said to me, 'These two sons of mine are blind, and this one daughter is deaf; how, brahmin, shall I comfort them now, and how shall I feed them?'
Saying this, he and his children sobbed and wept again and again; and the more that outcaste wept, the more pity rose in me.
Then, stopping his lament, I told him the story of his own family; and in his sorrow he entered Kokamukha together with his children, stricken.
As soon as Matanga entered the water he was freed from sin by the power of the tirtha, and mounting a celestial car as bright as the moon, he went to heaven while I watched, father.
When he had entered the water and died, a bewildering anguish came over me; then, O best of kings, I entered the water of the most holy Koka and went to heaven.

Again I was born in a merchant family, afflicted with pain but remembering my past births by the grace of that excellent tirtha; then, deeply dispassionate, I went to Kokamukha, restrained in speech and mind.
Undertaking a vow and wasting away my body, I ascended to heaven; falling from there I was born in your house, father, remembering my past births by Hari's grace.
So I shall worship the god Murari at Kokamukha, having given up desire for good and ill." Having said this, he bowed to his father and went to Kokamukha, foremost of tirthas.
Thus Kamadamana, with his sons and grandsons, gave up his faulty body at the most holy, excellent tirtha of Kokamukha, and then went to heaven in celestial cars as bright as the sun.
So I have described the maya of the Supreme Lord, inconceivable even to the gods — Murari's maya, like a dream or a magic show, by which the world falls into delusion, O brahmins.
Living on roots, leaves and fruits like ascetics, men afflicted by drought will then kill themselves.
In the Kali age helpless men will constantly suffer famine and hardship, their happiness blocked through their own negligence.
When Kali comes, they will eat without bathing, and will not worship the fire, the gods or guests, nor perform the offerings of rice-balls and water.
In Kali women will be greedy, short in stature, given to eating much, with many children and little fortune.
Scratching their heads with both hands, women will unveiled disobey the commands of elders and husbands.
In Kali women will care only for feeding themselves, be quick to anger, neglect the care of their bodies, and speak harsh and false words.
Women of good family will be ill-behaved, constantly longing for men of wicked character, and of bad conduct.
Students will take up the Vedas without keeping vows; householders will not offer oblations nor give even what is proper.
Forest-dwellers will take to village food and possessions, and mendicants will be bound by the machinery of affection for sons.
When the Kali age arrives, kings will not protect but plunder, seizing people's wealth under the pretext of taxes.
In the Kali age whoever is rich in horses, chariots and elephants will be king, and whoever is weak will be a servant.
Vaishyas, giving up their own work of farming and trade, will live like Shudras, earning by crafts.
Likewise low Shudras will take up the vow of begging and wear the marks of renunciants; uninitiated, they will adopt a livelihood based on heresy.
Greatly oppressed by famine and taxes, people in distress will move to lands where wheat and barley are eaten.
When the Vedic path has vanished and people are full of heresy, the lifespan of the worlds will become short through the growth of unrighteousness.
When men practise terrible austerities not sanctioned by scripture, children will die young because of the king's faults.
In Kali women will give birth at five, six or seven years of age, and men will father children at eight, nine or ten.
Grey hair will appear at twelve; in Kali no one will live to twenty years.
In Kali men of little understanding, bearing marks without meaning and wicked at heart, will perish here and there in a short time.
Whenever heretical conduct is seen here, the wise should infer that Kali is increasing.
Whenever the good who follow the Vedic path decline, the wise should infer that Kali is increasing.
When the undertakings of men who practise dharma fail, the wise should infer, O brahmins, that Kali prevails.
Whenever men do not worship with sacrifices the Supreme Person, Lord of sacrifices, then the strength of Kali should be recognized.
When there is no love for the words of the Veda and delight in heresies, the wise should infer the growth of Kali, O best of brahmins.
In Kali, O brahmins, men struck down by heresy will not worship Vishnu, Lord of the world, the creator of all, the Supreme Lord.
What are gods, brahmins and Vedas to us? What is purity with water? — so will men struck down by heresy prattle.
When the Kali age comes, O brahmins, the clouds will give little rain, crops will yield little, and fruit will have little substance.
In the Kali age clothes will mostly be knee-length, trees mostly shami, and the classes mostly like Shudras.
When Kali comes, grains will be mostly tiny, milk mostly goat's milk, and ushira the only unguent.
In Kali men's elders will mostly be their mothers- and fathers-in-law, and their friends the brothers of their wives, O best of sages.
Whose mother, whose father? A man is only his own deeds — so will men who follow their fathers-in-law declare.
Overcome again and again by faults of speech, mind and body, men of little intelligence will commit sins day after day.
For those without truth, without purity and without shame, O brahmins, whatever brings sorrow will all come about in the Kali age.
When the world is without Vedic recitation and the cry of vashat, and devoid of svadha and svaha, a true brahmin will then be rare in the world.
Yet in that age one gains in a short time the unsurpassed mass of merit that in the Krita age is gained through austerity."
In which age does a little dharma give very great fruit? Please tell us fully; we long to hear.

Blessed is Kali, O brahmins, in which great fruit comes with little hardship; and blessed too are women and Shudras. Learn something more:
brahmapuran:230:62	what is gained in Krita by ten years, in Treta by one year, and in Dvapara by a month, is gained in Kali by a day and a night.
brahmapuran:230:63	The fruit of austerity, celibacy, japa and the like, O brahmins, a man attains quickly in Kali; that is why I said 'Well done' to it.
brahmapuran:230:64	What one gains in Krita by meditation, in Treta by sacrifices and in Dvapara by worship, one gains in Kali by chanting the name of Keshava.
brahmapuran:230:65	In Kali a man gains the highest excellence of dharma with very little effort, O knowers of dharma; that is why I am pleased with Kali.
brahmapuran:230:66	In earlier ages the twice-born had to receive the Vedas while devoted to strict vows, and then, having gained dharma, sacrifice duly with wealth.
brahmapuran:230:67	Idle talk, idle eating and idle wealth bring the twice-born to a fall, so they must live in constant restraint.
brahmapuran:230:68	In all things they incur faults by doing them improperly; even their food and drink do not come as they wish, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:230:69	Being dependent in all their duties, they win their worlds with great hardship and humility.
brahmapuran:230:70	The Shudra, entitled to the simple domestic sacrifices, wins his own world merely by serving the twice-born; so he is the more fortunate.
brahmapuran:230:71	Since for him there are no strict rules about what may and may not be eaten, or about sins, O tigers among sages, he was called 'blessed.'
brahmapuran:230:72	Men must always gain wealth without violating their own dharma, give it to worthy recipients, and sacrifice according to rule.
brahmapuran:230:73	There is great hardship in earning it and in keeping it, O best of brahmins, and using it rightly is known to be difficult for men.
brahmapuran:230:74	Through these and other hardships, O best of brahmins, men win their own worlds, the world of Prajapati and the rest, in due order.
brahmapuran:230:75	A woman, by serving her husband in deed, mind and speech, attains the same goal, since she shares his world, O brahmins,
brahmapuran:230:76	without the great hardship that a man undergoes; that is why I said the third thing, 'Blessed are women.'
brahmapuran:230:77	This I have told you, brahmins, concerning what you came here for; now ask as you wish, and I will answer you clearly.
brahmapuran:230:78	In Kali dharma is accomplished with very little effort by men who have washed away all their sins with the waters of their own virtues,
brahmapuran:230:79	by Shudras devoted to serving the twice-born, O best of sages, and by women effortlessly, simply through serving their husbands.
brahmapuran:230:80	Therefore these three I consider most blessed. For the twice-born in Krita and the other ages the pursuit of dharma is hard,
brahmapuran:230:81	but in this age men will attain perfection with little austerity; the blessed will practise dharma at the end of the ages, O best of sages.
brahmapuran:230:82	What you had in mind I have told you even without being asked, O knowers of dharma; what else shall be done, brahmins?
Kshatriyas will live by wealth and grain like Vaishyas; as the age declines, kinsmen will no longer be kinsmen.
Agreements and oaths will be seen to lapse; when the age wanes, debts will be repaid without courtesy, or not at all.
Men's joy will bear no fruit and their anger will bear fruit; at the end of the age even goats will be tethered for their milk.
Sacrifice will be performed in ways not sanctioned by scripture; men who think themselves learned will treat authority as nothing.
No doubt they will not teach what the scriptures say; everyone will think he knows everything, without having served the elders.
When the end of the age arrives, no one will call himself unlearned; the stars will be out of their conjunctions, and the twice-born will not keep to their duties.
When the end of the age arrives, kings will be little better than thieves; brahmins will be adulterers' sons, deceitful, and drinkers of liquor, while talking of Brahman.
At the end of the age, O best of brahmins, they will perform the horse-sacrifice; they will officiate for those unfit to sacrifice and eat what should not be eaten.
When the end of the age arrives, brahmins tormented by thirst for wealth will call out "Bho!" to one another, but none will study.
Women will wear a single conch bangle and be clothed in gavedhuka grass; the stars will lose their colour and the ten directions will be reversed.
At the end of the age the twilight glow will look like burnt limbs; sons will send their fathers, and daughters-in-law their mothers-in-law, to work.
So will women and men live in those ages; brahmins will eat without offering the first portion and without tending their fires.
Men will eat by themselves without giving alms or bali offerings; women will deceive their sleeping husbands and go to others.
When the age wanes, no one will care for the sick, the unsightly, the diligent or even the envious, nor will anyone repay a kindness.

When dharma has thus faltered, where will men oppressed by taxes live, and on what food and pastimes?
brahmapuran:231:43	What will be their work, their aims, their stature and their lifespan? And reaching what limit will they come to the Krita age?

After that, when dharma has fallen and people are without virtue, they will fall into vices of conduct and their lifespan will decline.
brahmapuran:231:45	With loss of lifespan comes loss of strength; with loss of strength, loss of colour; from loss of colour, affliction by disease; and from affliction by disease, weariness of the world.
brahmapuran:231:46	From weariness comes self-awakening, and from awakening, devotion to dharma; having thus reached the furthest limit, they will come to the Krita age.
brahmapuran:231:47	Some will be righteous in name only, some will remain indifferent; some will ask 'What is dharma?', and some here will be merely curious.
brahmapuran:231:48	Some, convinced that only perception and inference are valid means of knowledge, and other people, will treat everything as without authority.
brahmapuran:231:49	Some deluded men, O brahmins, thinking themselves learned, will be given to unbelief and will destroy dharma.
brahmapuran:231:50	Trusting only in the present moment, excluded from knowledge of the scriptures, those men will be hypocrites, their knowledge lost.
brahmapuran:231:51	Yet even when dharma is so disturbed, people who honour the best will practise good deeds, devoted to generosity and good conduct.
brahmapuran:231:52	People will then eat everything, look only to themselves, and be pitiless and shameless — that is the mark of the dregs of the age.
brahmapuran:231:53	At the time of the dregs' onslaught, when devotion to knowledge is destroyed, those who are unadorned will attain perfection in a short time.
brahmapuran:231:54	When people of the lowest class resort to the everlasting livelihood of brahmins, O brahmins, that is the mark of the dregs.
brahmapuran:231:55	Great war, great rain, great wind and great heat will come as the age wanes — that is the mark of the dregs.
brahmapuran:231:56	When the end of the age arrives, Yakshas in the guise of brahmins, and kings who heed only tale-bearers, will enjoy the earth.
brahmapuran:231:57	Without Vedic study or the vashat cry, poor leaders and arrogant, flesh-eaters in the guise of brahmins, eating everything, with pointless vows,
brahmapuran:231:58	foolish, bent on wealth, greedy, mean, with mean possessions, occupied in trade, fallen from the eternal dharma,
brahmapuran:231:59	stealers of others' jewels, violators of others' wives, lustful, evil-minded, deceitful and fond of violence —
brahmapuran:231:60	when such people prevail everywhere, sages of many forms will come into being who are of no account.
brahmapuran:231:61	Those who arise as leading men in the Kali age, people will honour them all merely for their talk.
brahmapuran:231:62	There will be thieves of crops and stealers of clothes, stealers of food and eatables, and stealers of baskets.
brahmapuran:231:63	Thieves will rob thieves, and killers will kill killers; and when thieves have destroyed thieves, there will be safety.
brahmapuran:231:64	In that worthless, agitated time, when things stand idle, men oppressed by the burden of taxes will take refuge in the forests.
brahmapuran:231:65	When sacrificial rites have ceased, Rakshasas and beasts of prey, insects, rats and snakes will assail men.
brahmapuran:231:66	As the age wanes, men will be 'best' only in name in matters of safety, plenty, health and wholeness among kinsmen.
brahmapuran:231:67	Their own guards and their own thieves, laden with gear for flight, they will form separate bands in every land.
brahmapuran:231:68	Then, with the decline of the age, all men will be driven from their own lands, stripped of substance, together with their kin.
brahmapuran:231:69	Then all, taking their children and fleeing in fear, will cross the Kaushiki, tormented by hunger and fear.
brahmapuran:231:70	People will take refuge in Anga, Vanga, Kalinga, Kashmira and Koshala, and in the valleys of the mountains at the sages' borders.
brahmapuran:231:71	The whole flank of the Himalaya and the shore of the salt ocean — making for themselves various garments of old leaves, bark and hides,
brahmapuran:231:72	they will dwell there when the age has ended; men will live in the forests together with bands of Mlecchas.
brahmapuran:231:73	The earth will be neither empty nor newly forested; kings who do not protect will become protectors.
brahmapuran:231:74	Men will live on deer, fish, birds, beasts of prey, snakes and insects, on honey, herbs, fruits and roots.
brahmapuran:231:75	Eating withered leaves and fruits, making bark garments and hides for themselves, they will live as the sages do.
brahmapuran:231:76	Without care for seeds, turning the soil with wooden stakes, they will always tend goats and sheep, donkeys and camels.
brahmapuran:231:77	Settling on the banks for the sake of water, they will dam the streams of rivers, trading with one another in cooked food.
brahmapuran:231:78	With hair as it grows, full of dirt within, having many children yet without descendants, without family or good conduct —
brahmapuran:231:79	so will men be then, living by unrighteousness; people will follow a dharma lower and lower.
brahmapuran:231:80	The lifespan of mortals there will be thirty years at most; they will be weak, wearied by sense objects, and overwhelmed by old age and grief.
brahmapuran:231:81	Then their senses will decay through disease, and with the checking of life's supports they will turn away from sense objects.
brahmapuran:231:82	They will become eager to serve and delight in seeing the good, and will take to truth as their dealings dwindle.
brahmapuran:231:83	Through failing to obtain their desires they will become righteous, and, afflicted by decline, will themselves perform the sacraments.
brahmapuran:231:84	Thus becoming eager for giving, truth and the protection of living beings, when dharma begins to move again on one foot, good will return.
brahmapuran:231:85	For those who have gained discernment and turn toward virtues, knowing what is truly sweet, dharma alone is seen.
brahmapuran:231:86	Just as they came to decline step by step, so they go on to prosperity step by step; and when dharma is taken up, they behold the Krita age.
brahmapuran:231:87	Good conduct is said to belong to the Krita age, and decline to the age of dregs; yet it is one and the same time, like the moon that has lost its colour.
brahmapuran:231:88	As the moon covered by darkness, so is the Kali age; and as the moon freed from darkness, so is the Krita age.
brahmapuran:231:89	The Arthavada they know as the supreme Brahman and the meaning of the Veda; undiscerned and unknown, it is held here only as an inheritance.
brahmapuran:231:90	Austerity is said to be the doctrine of reward, and austerity has grown old; works come about through the qualities, and the qualities are purified by works.
brahmapuran:231:91	Blessings, suited to the person, place and time, have been declared by the sages in every age according to the time.
brahmapuran:231:92	So too in every age are the remedies concerning dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation and the gods, the holy and auspicious blessings, and the lifespan.
brahmapuran:231:93	Thus the turnings of the ages have gone on for long by the nature of the ordinance; the world of living beings does not stand still for a moment, turning through decline and rise.
brahmapuran:232:13	Hear from me, O best of brahmins, its very fearsome nature; I will tell of the natural dissolution again, and then of the final absorption.
brahmapuran:232:14	At the end of a thousand four-age cycles, when the earth is nearly exhausted, a terrible drought arises lasting a hundred years.
brahmapuran:232:15	Then the many beings of the earth that have little strength perish, O best of sages, from the extreme affliction.
brahmapuran:232:16	Then the blessed Krishna, imperishable, taking the form of Rudra, sets about destroying all creatures and drawing them into himself.
brahmapuran:232:17	Then the blessed Vishnu, dwelling in the seven rays of the sun, drinks up all the waters, O best of sages.
brahmapuran:232:18	Having drunk all the waters, including those in living beings, he dries up the whole surface of the earth, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:232:19	The oceans, rivers, mountains and mountain springs, and whatever water is in the netherworlds — all this he brings to destruction.
brahmapuran:232:20	Then, strengthened by feeding on that water, seven suns with a thousand rays arise there.
brahmapuran:232:21	Blazing below and above, those seven suns then burn the entire three worlds together with the netherworlds, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:232:22	Burned by those blazing suns, the three worlds, with their mountains, trees and expanse of oceans, become utterly dry.
brahmapuran:232:23	Then, its trees and waters burnt up, the whole of the three worlds and this earth take on the shape of a tortoise's back.
brahmapuran:232:24	Then Hara as Kalagni-Rudra, the destroyer of creation, burns the netherworlds below with the heat of the breath of the serpent Shesha.
brahmapuran:232:25	That great fire, having burned all the netherworlds, reaches the earth and burns the whole surface of the ground;
brahmapuran:232:26	then the terrible whirling mass of flames rolls over the whole of Bhuvarloka and Svarloka.
brahmapuran:232:27	The entire three worlds then look like a frying pan, surrounded by whirling flames, and their strength wanes.
brahmapuran:232:28	Then the dwellers of the two worlds, overcome by heat and left without room, go to Maharloka, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:232:29	Scorched by the great heat even there, those beings, seeking a higher refuge, go on to Janaloka.
brahmapuran:232:30	Then Janardana in the form of Rudra, having burned the whole world, creates clouds from the breath of his mouth, O best of sages.
brahmapuran:232:31	Then the terrible Samvartaka clouds rise in the sky like herds of elephants, flashing with lightning and thundering.
brahmapuran:232:32	Some are black as collyrium, some like white lotuses; some clouds are smoke-coloured, some rain-clouds yellow;
brahmapuran:232:33	some have the colour of turmeric, some are like lac-dye; some are like lapis lazuli, some like sapphire;
brahmapuran:232:34	others are like conch and kunda flowers, or like jasmine; some like cochineal insects, some like red arsenic;
brahmapuran:232:35	some dense clouds rise like lotus leaves; some have the shape of great cities, some are like mountains;
brahmapuran:232:36	others are like mansions, some like plains; huge and loudly roaring, they fill the sky.
brahmapuran:232:37	Pouring down in great torrents, they quench that most fearful fire spread throughout the three worlds, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:232:38	And when the fire is extinguished, those clouds rain for more than a hundred years, flooding the whole world, O best of sages.
brahmapuran:232:39	With streams as thick as axle-poles they flood the whole earth, and likewise Bhuvarloka above, and heaven, O brahmins.
brahmapuran:232:40	When the world has been plunged into darkness and all moving and unmoving things have perished, those great clouds rain for more than a hundred years.
brahmapuran:233:15	When the subtle element of smell has vanished, the earth becomes water; then the waters rush forth, swift and roaring,
brahmapuran:233:16	and fill all this, standing still and moving about; the Lokaloka mountain on every side is covered by the billowing waters.
brahmapuran:233:17	The quality of the waters is then drunk up by fire; the waters, heated, perish through the loss of the subtle element of taste.
brahmapuran:233:18	Then the waters, whose essence is taste, become fire; when the water has become fire and everything is enveloped by radiance,
brahmapuran:233:19	that fire, pervading everywhere, takes up the water; and gradually this whole world is filled with its flames.
brahmapuran:233:20	When it is spread with flames across, above and below, wind consumes the form of fire, the maker of light.
brahmapuran:233:21	When that fire has dissolved into wind, the self of all, and the subtle element of form has vanished, fire loses its form
brahmapuran:233:22	and the light dies away; then the great wind blows violently. When the world is without light and fire has merged into wind,
brahmapuran:233:23	the wind, having come to dissolution into its own source, shakes the ten directions above and across.
brahmapuran:233:24	Then space swallows touch, the quality of wind; the wind subsides, and space remains unenclosed —
brahmapuran:233:25	without form, taste, touch or smell, and without shape; it shines forth immense, filling all.
brahmapuran:233:26	All around, that space whose mark is sound, space consisting of sound alone, remains, enveloping everything.
brahmapuran:233:27	Then the elemental ego swallows sound, its quality; when the elements and senses have together come to rest in the elemental ego,
brahmapuran:233:28	this elemental ego, whose nature is self-conception and which is called tamasa, is itself swallowed by the discerning Great Intellect (Mahat).
brahmapuran:233:29	Earth and Mahat are the outer and inner limits of the world; thus the seven principles, down to the Great Intellect, in due order
brahmapuran:233:30	all enter one another by withdrawal, and the egg by which all this is enveloped dissolves into the waters.
brahmapuran:233:31	The seven continents and oceans, the seven worlds with their mountains — the covering of water here is drunk up by fire.
brahmapuran:233:32	Fire dissolves into wind, wind into space; the elemental ego swallows space, and Mahat swallows it.
brahmapuran:233:33	Prakriti swallows Mahat together with all these, O brahmins; the equilibrium of the qualities, neither in excess nor deficient, O best of brahmins,
brahmapuran:233:34	is called Prakriti, the cause, Pradhana, the supreme cause; this Prakriti is entirely of manifest and unmanifest nature.
brahmapuran:233:35	The manifest dissolves into her unmanifest nature, O brahmins. The one who is pure, imperishable, eternal and all-pervading —
brahmapuran:233:36	he too is a portion of the Supreme Self of all beings, O best of brahmins, in whom all notions of name, class and the like vanish;
brahmapuran:233:37	in the Supreme Self, which is to be known as pure existence and whose nature is knowledge — that is Brahman, the supreme abode, the Supreme Self, the highest Lord.
brahmapuran:233:38	He is Vishnu, all this universe, from whom there is no return. The Prakriti I have described, of manifest and unmanifest nature,
brahmapuran:233:39	and the Purusha — both these dissolve into the Supreme Self; and the Supreme Self is the support of all, the Supreme Lord.
brahmapuran:233:40	He is sung in the Vedas and the Vedanta by the name of Vishnu. Vedic action is of two kinds, of engagement and of withdrawal;
brahmapuran:233:41	through both of these men worship him as the embodiment of sacrifice. He is worshipped through the paths of engagement, with the Rig, Yajur and Sama Vedas —
brahmapuran:233:42	the Lord of sacrifice, the Person of sacrifice, the Supreme Person — by men; and as the Self of knowledge, the embodiment of knowledge, he is worshipped through the yoga of knowledge.
brahmapuran:233:43	Through the paths of withdrawal and yoga Vishnu grants the fruit of liberation. Whatever thing is named with short, long or prolonged syllables,
brahmapuran:233:44	and whatever lies beyond the reach of words — all that is the imperishable Vishnu. He is the manifest, he is the unmanifest, he is the imperishable Person,
brahmapuran:233:45	the Supreme Self, the Self of the universe, Hari who bears the form of the universe. Into him that Prakriti of manifest and unmanifest nature dissolves,
brahmapuran:233:46	and the Purusha too, O brahmins, into that undifferentiated Self. The time I have described as two parardhas, O brahmins,
brahmapuran:233:47	is called the day of that Lord Vishnu, O best of brahmins; and when the manifest has dissolved into Prakriti, and Prakriti into Purusha,
brahmapuran:233:48	and it remains so, that is his night of the same measure, O ascetics. Yet for the eternal Supreme Self there is neither day nor night;
brahmapuran:233:49	it is only figuratively said of that Lord. This, O tigers among sages, is the natural (prakrita) dissolution I have described.
brahmapuran:234:23	What is dharma and what is adharma? In what state should one be, and how? What is to be done and what not? What has merit and what has fault? —
